summary:
Chaco province has no statute of its own on legal gender recognition, and the record contains no provincial criminalisation provision, enforcement series or quota-compliance finding. A trans visitor to Chaco therefore stands under Argentina's national framework: Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal of the statute. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors, and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

Institutional protection machinery has been dismantled at national level. The federal anti-discrimination agency INADI has been closed, the Ministry of Women, Gender and Diversity has been eliminated, and trans people hired under the public-sector labour-inclusion quota were dismissed in 2024. Trans activists interviewed in Buenos Aires by the Washington Blade on 10 April 2025 described the community's situation as chaotic and desperate, with violence, discrimination and poverty reported as worsened. Chaco carries no separate reporting, so the national picture stands as the baseline for the province.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a 62% increase on the previous year and the highest count in the observatory's ten years of operation, averaging one crime every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis made up 62.5% of victims, 142 cases, and gay men 22%, 50 cases. Agencia Presentes reported the figures on 19 March 2026 and tied the surge to institutional weakening and state legitimation of discriminatory discourse.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, but rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeal court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated-crime aggravator therefore does not apply in the case as it now stands.

Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010, the first Latin American country to do so, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws. An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration.
tangentialFactors:
The 2025 hate-crime total is the highest recorded by the National LGBT+ Hate Crimes Observatory across its ten years of operation, and the 62% year-on-year rise marks a break with the earlier trajectory of the series rather than a continuation of it.

Argentina was long treated as the regional reference point for transgender rights: the United Nations described Law 26.743 as a pioneering step, and the country was the first in Latin America to legalise marriage equality. The current national picture, with the anti-discrimination agency closed, the diversity ministry eliminated and a record year for hate crimes, runs against that standing.

Chaco appears in none of the source material as a site of trans-specific violence, litigation or policy change. Findings for the province are inherited from the national pattern, and the province should not be read as either an exception to it or as an independently documented case.
localsOnly:
Residents of Chaco who change their legal gender under Law 26.743 do so without surgery, hormone treatment or a court order, and the process is governed by national registry rules rather than any provincial procedure.

Trans residents employed in Chaco's public sector were among those affected by the 2024 dismissal of people hired under the national labour-inclusion quota, which was a quota measure rather than a provincial employment decision.

The closure of INADI removes the federal complaint channel that residents previously used for discrimination claims; provincial anti-discrimination provisions remain in force and are the residual domestic recourse.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the constitutional litigation against the February 2025 decree restricting gender-affirming care for minors is unresolved in the sources available here, so the decree's current operative status cannot be stated.

No source records how the second February 2025 decree, on the housing of transgender people in prison, has been applied in Chaco, and no Chaco-specific prison or detention data is available.

There is no Chaco-specific record of hate crimes, police conduct, or document-processing delays for trans residents; the province's figures are not separately tracked in the national observatory data cited here.
